IMMIGRATION-RELATED UNFAIR EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

DECLARATION OF PARTIES AND THE PRACTICE ALLEGED
This Immigration-Related Unfair Employment Practices — Information Sheet concerns a possible charge under 8 U.S.C. § 1324b involving Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee. The unfair immigration-related employment practice identified is described as: refusal to accept a facially valid work authorization document. The date of the incident identified is October 1, 2026. Additional incidents (if any): On March 10, 2026, the respondent sent several threatening text messages to the petitioner. This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual charge submitted to the Office of Special Counsel for Immigration-Related Unfair Employment Practices, U.S. Department of Justice; it is not itself a charge, and completing it does not file a charge with the Special Counsel, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, or any other agency. Only a charge actually submitted to the Special Counsel — in writing, under oath or affirmation — does that.

THE THREE CATEGORIES OF PROHIBITED CONDUCT UNDER § 1324B(A)(1)
8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(1) makes it an unfair immigration-related employment practice for a person or other entity to discriminate against an individual with respect to three specific employment actions: hiring, recruitment or referral for a fee, and discharging the individual from employment. The statute draws a distinction in whose protection applies to which basis: discrimination because of national origin is prohibited as to any individual other than an unauthorized alien, while discrimination because of citizenship status is prohibited only as to a narrower, separately defined category called a "protected individual." National origin and citizenship status are treated as two distinct prohibited bases, each covering a different, specifically defined set of individuals.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "It is an unfair immigration-related employment practice for a person or other entity to discriminate against any individual (other than an unauthorized alien, as defined in section 1324a(h)(3) of this title) with respect to the hiring, or recruitment or referral for a fee, of the individual for employment or the discharging of the individual from employment— (A) because of such individual’s national origin, or (B) in the case of a protected individual (as defined in paragraph (3)), because of such individual’s citizenship status."
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, general prohibition on national-origin and citizenship-status discrimination (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324b)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory text, used as evidence of what § 1324b(a)(1) itself prohibits — not a claim about which basis or which employment action applies to any specific individual's actual situation, and not a claim that discrimination did or did not occur in fact. The quoted language is § 1324b(a)(1) alone; the statute's exceptions to this general rule (a small-employer exception, a Title VII-overlap exception for national-origin discrimination, and a law/contract-required exception for citizenship-status discrimination) and the definition of "protected individual" are addressed in the separate clauses of this document. "Unauthorized alien" is defined by cross-reference to 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(h)(3), a section this document does not independently verify or quote.

WHO QUALIFIES AS A "PROTECTED INDIVIDUAL"
8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(3) defines "protected individual" — the narrower category to whom the statute's citizenship-status protection applies — as an individual who is a citizen or national of the United States, or who is an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence, granted status as a lawfully admitted temporary resident under specific legalization provisions, admitted as a refugee, or granted asylum. That definition carries two statutory exclusions: an alien who fails to apply for naturalization within six months of first becoming eligible to do so is excluded, and an alien who applies on a timely basis but is not naturalized within two years of the application is also excluded — unless that alien can establish active pursuit of naturalization, in which case time the government itself spends processing the application does not count against the two years.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "the term “protected individual” means an individual who— (A) is a citizen or national of the United States, or (B) is an alien who is lawfully admitted for permanent residence, is granted the status of an alien lawfully admitted for temporary residence under section 1160(a) or 1255a(a)(1) of this title, is admitted as a refugee under section 1157 of this title, or is granted asylum under section 1158 of this title; but does not include (i) an alien who fails to apply for naturalization within six months of the date the alien first becomes eligible (by virtue of period of lawful permanent residence) to apply for naturalization"
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, "protected individual" defined — categories and exclusion (i) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324b)
  "(ii) an alien who has applied on a timely basis, but has not been naturalized as a citizen within 2 years after the date of the application, unless the alien can establish that the alien is actively pursuing naturalization"
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, "protected individual" defined — exclusion (ii) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324b)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory text, used as evidence of the definition itself — not a determination of any specific individual's actual citizenship, national origin, or immigration status, and not an exhaustive restatement of every underlying category (for example, the specific temporary-residence legalization provisions cross-referenced, 8 U.S.C. §§ 1160(a) and 1255a(a)(1), are not independently verified or quoted here). Both citations below are to the same statutory paragraph, § 1324b(a)(3) — its main clause and exclusion (i), and its exclusion (ii) — not independent sources. This definition marks the outer limit of who § 1324b protects against citizenship-status discrimination specifically; the statute's broader national-origin protection covers a wider set of individuals (any individual other than an unauthorized alien), described in a separate clause of this document.

"DOCUMENT ABUSE" AS A DISTINCT PROHIBITED PRACTICE
Separately from the hiring/discharge discrimination described above, § 1324b(a)(6) makes it an unfair immigration-related employment practice for an employer, when carrying out Form I-9 verification, to request more or different documents than the verification statute requires, or to refuse to honor documents that reasonably appear genuine on their face — but only when that request or refusal is made for the purpose or with the intent of discriminating against an individual in violation of the core prohibition described above. This is commonly referred to as "document abuse." The statute treats it as a separately defined violation category: the civil-penalty range an administrative law judge may order specifically for a document-abuse violation is set at a different, generally lower dollar amount than the range for other § 1324b violations.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A person’s or other entity’s request, for purposes of satisfying the requirements of section 1324a(b) of this title, for more or different documents than are required under such section or refusing to honor documents tendered that on their face reasonably appear to be genuine shall be treated as an unfair immigration-related employment practice if made for the purpose or with the intent of discriminating against an individual in violation of paragraph (1)."
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(6) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, document-abuse practices (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324b)
  "in the case of an unfair immigration-related employment practice described in subsection (a)(6), to pay a civil penalty of not less than $100 and not more than $1,000 for each individual discriminated against"
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(g)(2)(B)(iv)(IV) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, separate civil-penalty range for document-abuse violations (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324b)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory text, used as evidence that document abuse is a defined, purpose-requiring violation category distinct from the general hiring/discharge prohibition — not a claim that any specific request for documents was, or was not, made with discriminatory intent. Both citations are to different provisions of the same statutory section, § 1324b — paragraph (a)(6) (the violation) and paragraph (g)(2)(B)(iv)(IV) (its penalty range) — not independent sources.

FILING A CHARGE WITH THE SPECIAL COUNSEL, AND THE 180-DAY DEADLINE
A charge alleging an unfair immigration-related employment practice under § 1324b is filed with the Special Counsel for Immigration-Related Unfair Employment Practices — an office within the U.S. Department of Justice, headed by a presidential appointee confirmed by the Senate to a four-year term. The charge may be filed by the person directly and adversely affected, by someone filing on that person's behalf, or by an officer of the relevant federal agency, and it must be in writing, under oath or affirmation. The statute sets a firm outer limit on timing: no complaint may later be filed regarding a practice that occurred more than 180 days before the charge was filed with the Special Counsel.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "any person alleging that the person is adversely affected directly by an unfair immigration-related employment practice (or a person on that person’s behalf) or an officer of the Service alleging that an unfair immigration-related employment practice has occurred or is occurring may file a charge respecting such practice or violation with the Special Counsel (appointed under subsection (c))."
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(b)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, who may file a charge and with whom (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324b)
  "The President shall appoint, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, a Special Counsel for Immigration-Related Unfair Employment Practices (hereinafter in this section referred to as the “Special Counsel”) within the Department of Justice to serve for a term of four years."
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(c)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Special Counsel's appointment and department (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324b)
  "No complaint may be filed respecting any unfair immigration-related employment practice occurring more than 180 days prior to the date of the filing of the charge with the Special Counsel."
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(d)(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, 180-day time limitation on complaints (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324b)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory text, used as evidence of the filing mechanism and the 180-day limitation period themselves — not legal advice about whether any specific charge is or is not timely, and not a claim about how the 180-day count applies to a continuing practice or a later-discovered practice. The three citations below are to three different subsections of the same statutory section, § 1324b — (b)(1) (who may file, and with whom), (c)(1) (the Special Counsel's appointment and department), and (d)(3) (the 180-day limit) — not independent sources. Section 1324b(b)(2) also bars filing the same set of facts as both a § 1324b charge and an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission charge under Title VII, addressed further in the employer-size clause of this document; this document does not verify the separate EEOC charge-filing deadline under Title VII itself. The statutory text refers to "the Service" (the former Immigration and Naturalization Service) for certain investigative-officer references; this document does not independently verify the successor agency structure under the current Department of Homeland Security.

REMEDIES AN ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGE MAY ORDER
If, after a hearing, an administrative law judge determines by a preponderance of the evidence that a person or entity has engaged in an unfair immigration-related employment practice, the judge must issue an order requiring that person or entity to cease and desist from the practice. The judge may also order additional remedies, including hiring the individuals directly and adversely affected, with or without back pay, and a civil penalty for each individual discriminated against — set, for a first-time violation other than document abuse, at not less than $250 and not more than $2,000 per individual, with higher statutory ranges for repeat violators and a separate, lower range specifically for document-abuse violations. Back pay is limited: it cannot accrue from a date more than two years before the charge was filed with the Special Counsel, and interim earnings reduce whatever back pay would otherwise be owed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "the judge shall state his findings of fact and shall issue and cause to be served on such person or entity an order which requires such person or entity to cease and desist from such unfair immigration-related employment practice."
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(g)(2)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, mandatory cease-and-desist order (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324b)
  "to hire individuals directly and adversely affected, with or without back pay"
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(g)(2)(B)(iii) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, hiring with or without back pay (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324b)
  "to pay a civil penalty of not less than $250 and not more than $2,000 for each individual discriminated against"
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(g)(2)(B)(iv)(I) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, first-tier civil-penalty range (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324b)
  "back pay liability shall not accrue from a date more than two years prior to the date of the filing of a charge with the Special Counsel"
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(g)(2)(C) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, back-pay accrual limit (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324b)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory text, used as evidence of the available remedies and the dollar figures and time limits the statute itself attaches to them — not a claim about what remedy, if any, a judge would order in a specific case, and not the complete remedy list: the statute also authorizes notice-posting, personnel-training, personnel-file-correction, and record-retention orders, not quoted here. All four citations below are to different provisions within the same statutory subsection, § 1324b(g) — (g)(2)(A) (the cease-and-desist requirement), (g)(2)(B)(iii) (hiring with back pay), (g)(2)(B)(iv)(I) (the first-tier civil-penalty range), and (g)(2)(C) (the back-pay limitation) — not independent sources. The civil-penalty dollar figures quoted are the amounts set out in the statutory text itself; this document does not independently verify whether a later inflation-adjustment regulation — which federal civil-penalty statutes are periodically required to receive — has since revised these figures upward, so an actually-assessed penalty today may differ from the statutory figures quoted here.

EMPLOYER-SIZE THRESHOLD, AND HOW IT RELATES TO TITLE VII
Section 1324b(a)(1)'s general prohibition does not apply to a person or entity that employs three or fewer employees — so, on its face, the statute's protection reaches only employers with four or more employees. The statute also withdraws its own national-origin-discrimination coverage where the same person or entity and the same individual are already covered, for that same discrimination, under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Title VII's own coverage is not universal: a separate federal statute, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(b), defines a covered Title VII "employer" as one with fifteen or more employees for each working day in each of twenty or more calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar year. Read together, these two statutes leave a specific band of employers — more than three but fewer than fifteen employees — where § 1324b's national-origin protection applies but Title VII's does not.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Paragraph (1) shall not apply to— (A) a person or other entity that employs three or fewer employees"
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(2)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, three-or-fewer-employee exception (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324b)
  "a person’s or entity’s discrimination because of an individual’s national origin if the discrimination with respect to that person or entity and that individual is covered under section 703 of the Civil Rights Act of 1964"
  — 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(2)(B) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Title VII-overlap exception for national-origin discrimination (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1324b)
  "The term “employer” means a person engaged in an industry affecting commerce who has fifteen or more employees for each working day in each of twenty or more calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar year"
  — 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(b) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Title VII "employer" defined — fifteen-employee threshold (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/2000e)
  Known gap: The first two citations below are to two different paragraphs of the same statutory subsection, § 1324b(a)(2) — the three-or-fewer-employee exception and the Title VII-overlap exception — not independent sources; the third citation, to 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(b), is a genuinely independent statute (a different U.S. Code title, from a different Act, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964) confirming the fifteen-employee figure used above. This clause states what the two statutes' employee-count thresholds are and how they interact on their face; it is not a claim that Title VII does or does not apply to any specific employer, which also depends on facts such as whether the employer is "engaged in an industry affecting commerce" and the applicable calendar-week count, not verified here. Citizenship-status discrimination has no comparable Title VII-overlap exception: § 1324b(a)(2)(B)'s overlap exception is expressly limited to discrimination "because of an individual's national origin," so on this statute's text the three-or-fewer-employee threshold is the only employer-size boundary that applies to § 1324b's citizenship-status protection.

expectedJSON.gap: The first two citations below are to two different paragraphs of the same statutory subsection, § 1324b(a)(2) — the three-or-fewer-employee exception and the Title VII-overlap exception — not independent sources; the third citation, to 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(b), is a genuinely independent statute (a different U.S. Code title, from a different Act, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964) confirming the fifteen-employee figure used above. This clause states what the two statutes' employee-count thresholds are and how they interact on their face; it is not a claim that Title VII does or does not apply to any specific employer, which also depends on facts such as whether the employer is "engaged in an industry affecting commerce" and the applicable calendar-week count, not verified here. Citizenship-status discrimination has no comparable Title VII-overlap exception: § 1324b(a)(2)(B)'s overlap exception is expressly limited to discrimination "because of an individual's national origin," so on this statute's text the three-or-fewer-employee threshold is the only employer-size boundary that applies to § 1324b's citizenship-status protection.
